newsitem.title: USA: Apple has new software strategy - CEO.
newsitem.headline: Apple has new software strategy - CEO.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc., which in the past has often given away its most valuable software, is embarking on a new software strategy as it seeks to reverse a string of losses and rebuild.

Gilbert Amelio, Apple's chairman since February, said in an interview Monday that he was working to update the business model for Apple which he said was still stuck in a 1984 mindset, the year that Apple launched the Macintosh.
Amelio also said the troubled computer maker's restructuring was on schedule and that his biggest accomplishment so far has been "that we survived."
"I think we've got a hell of a lot done in the past eight months," said Amelio, who was brought in by Apple's board in February to turn around the ailing computer maker.

"I am most proud of the fact that we survived," he said in response to a question during an interview. He said he still expected the computer maker to report a profit for its fiscal second quarter that ends in March 1997.
"I have no reason to believe we won't do that," he said.

Part of Amelio's strategy has been focusing on what Apple does best, which is developing an easy-to-use computer "for the rest of us." It was Apple's treasured operating system that for years made the Mac easier to use than other PCs, before Windows took off.

"In the beginning, customers valued hardware, so that's what they wanted to pay for," Amelio told Reuters. "Over time, customers' perception has shifted to where their view of hardware is pretty much as a commodity ... and that the value is in other the stuff -- but we don't charge for the other stuff."
Amelio said Apple planned to sell customers incremental releases of its operating system where custmers can update their programs as needed.

This so-called "modular release" of select pieces of its operating system and other software will generate a whole new source of revenue. Software could account for as much as half of total revenues in about five years, Amelio said.

Apple does not split its revenues now between hardware and software, because its software, such as its much-vaunted Macintosh operating system, is bundled free with each Macintosh, as is its QuickTime video playback software.
Apple will begin the new strategy in January, when it releases part of an upgrade to its current 7.5 version of the Mac operating system, code-named Harmony.
The modular software upgrade will hopefully stave off users who have been waiting for Apple's Copland, the much-anticipated revamp of the Macintosh operating system that has been fraught with delays.
Amelio said Apple was still working on fixing the core "plumbing," the foundation layer of Copland, but he did not give any time frame on when or how it would be released.
Amelio said the stragegy for revamping the foundation of Copland will include making it compatible with its other Macintosh applications.

He said the model is somewhat analogous to Netscape Communications Corp.'s use of "plug-ins" for its Navigator browser software, where users can download software additions. For example, users can add new software to the browser to allow long-distance calling over the Internet.
Amelio, who took over Apple in February, also said that he expected these new software products to be highly profitable, but he declined to be more specific.

"We have to get a certain price for the business model to make sense," Amelio said, adding that Apple will probably continue to bundle the core operating system free with the hardware, but users will pay for any new features they want.
Amelio also said that Apple has a half a dozen exciting hardware and software products for 1997, but he said he did not want to preannounce products.
Despite being popular with some users, Apple machines have been losing out to computers from competitors and the Cupertino, Calif.-based company has been hit by heavy losses.
Apple lost $32 million in its fiscal third quarter after reporting a record $740 million loss in the second quarter, which included one-time charges for its massive restructuring program.
